# VerityOps — Hallucination / Risk Classifier: Model Report

**All data is synthetic.** Generated by `src/generate_data.py` (seed 42, n=2,400). No real Canon data is used.

- Champion model: **Logistic Regression** (selected on test F1, tie-broken by ROC-AUC)
- Test set: n=360, prevalence 29.7% hallucinated
- 5-fold CV ROC-AUC — Random Forest 0.8607 (±0.0089); Gradient Boosting 0.8458 (±0.0114)
- Time-based split ROC-AUC (Gradient Boosting, train ≤ 2026-03-31): 0.8241

## Honest limitations

- ~30% of synthetic hallucinations are SUBTLE (wrong problem description, or right part code with the wrong part name). No structured field contradicts them, so no grounding check can catch them — they cap recall. This mirrors reality: grounding checks catch factual contradictions, not plausible paraphrase.
- Summaries omit fields (~15% per field). A hallucination hiding in an omitted field is undetectable from the summary alone.
- Faithful summaries carry digit-transposition typos (~6%), so no single check is decisive; the model weighs evidence.
- The TF-IDF text-only model cannot see the source record, so it misses most numeric grounding errors — grounding checks against the work order are the core of the system, not the text model.
- Simulated LLM confidence overlaps heavily between classes; confidence alone must never auto-approve a summary.
- Time-split AUC is close to random-split AUC here, but on real data expect drift as the generator model is updated; monitor and retrain (see reports/monitoring.md).
- All data is synthetic and template-based; real LLM errors are more varied. Treat every metric above as a lower bound on real-world difficulty, not a production guarantee.

## How to reproduce

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
python run_all.py
```
Then inspect `reports/figures/`, `models/metrics.json`, and `reports/monitoring.md`.
